data.title: Why a shrinking population doesn't have to be the kiss of death for an economy or stock market
data.description:
By Mark Hulbert

Investors are all wrong about demography, a new study finds. Keep that in mind when allocating your portfolio.

I'm taking issue with the widespread belief that the long-term fates of a country's economy and stock market are closely tied to the size of its population. Though demographic determinism has a long history, in recent decades it perhaps has been most widely associated in the investment arena with financial analyst and author Harry Dent.

A new study questions this determinism. Titled "Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy," the study began circulating in academic circles this summer. Its authors are Daron Acemoglu, David Autor and Keelan Beirne of MIT and Andrew Scott of the London Business School. The authors found that "lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult" and that these two trends mostly cancel each other out - leaving a country's overall GDP largely unchanged as populations ebb and flow.

This finding may be good news for investors in countries whose populations are set to decline in coming decades. China's population in 2100 is projected to be more than 50% lower than today, for example, with Japan's 40% lower and Brazil's 23% smaller. If demography were destiny, then the long-term prospects of these countries' equities would be dismal.

Though the U.S. population is projected to grow modestly through 2100, the country is projected to fall from third to sixth place in a ranking of the world's most populous countries.

This new study will also be welcome news to investors in U.S. equities. Though the U.S. population is projected to grow modestly through 2100, the country is projected to fall from third to sixth place in a ranking of the world's most populous countries.

The study's authors effectively found that necessity is the mother of invention. When a country has a relative scarcity of younger workers, that country's technology sector rises to the occasion, resulting in "more labor-saving patents and growing high-tech activity." In addition, the authors found that countries with a relative shortage of workers experience faster growth in "Total Factor Productivity," which is the fraction of economic growth that can't be traced back to either labor or capital.

Many investors will react with incredulity, pointing to Japan as Exhibit A of why demography is destiny. The country's population was already plateauing by the late 1980s, when the Nikkei 225 (NIY00) stock average hit a peak that wasn't eclipsed for nearly four decades. The country's population today is lower than where it stood in the late 1980s and is projected to decline by nearly 40% more between now and the end of this century.

A glaring counterexample is South Korea. For many years it has been clear to demographers that its population was about to go over a cliff - yet its stock market has performed admirably. Its population hit a peak in 2020 and is projected to be 58% lower at the end of this century - even a bigger decline in percentage terms than in the case of China. And yet the iShares South Korea ETF EWY has held its own relative to the S&P 500 over the last couple of decades - even before this year, when South Korea's stock market has skyrocketed.

It is possible that other factors account for this new study's findings. Some have suggested that the bearish impact of a declining population can be avoided by an increasing share of women in the workforce and/or an increasingly educated workforce. But the researchers report that they found "little evidence" of support for these alternative explanations.

The investment implication of this new research is that long-term investors need not obsess about demographic projections when picking countries in which to invest. To illustrate, consider the accompanying chart that plots the relationship between the 20 largest developed countries' population growth over the 2000-25 period and the corresponding performance of their stock markets. Notice that the best-fit trend line is sloping slightly downward; though the angle of that slope is not a statistically significant difference from flat, the fact that it is downwardly sloping at all runs counter to what up until now has been the prevailing wisdom that an expanding population is a long-term economic positive.

The table below lists stocks of companies based outside the U.S. that currently are recommended by any of the investment newsletters monitored by my performance auditing firm. You'll notice that many of the companies are from countries with a projected population decline. If you had been avoiding such stocks because of what used to be the conventional wisdom, you can now consider each on its own merits rather than its country's demography - just as the newsletter editors already are doing.

Mark Hulbert is a regular contributor to MarketWatch. His Hulbert Ratings tracks investment newsletters that pay a flat fee to be audited. He can be reached at mark@hulbertratings.com

-Mark Hulbert

data.title: The traditional paths to building wealth are -2-
data.description:
Members of Gen Z said that on average it takes an annual income of $500,000 to be successful, more than twice the average amount cited by all respondents. Many want to retire earlier than previous generations did.

Faced with economic uncertainty, about 43% of Gen Z-ers now have a side hustle, according to a 2026 LendingTree survey. More than half of them see these gigs as supporting their long-term financial security, and 35% plan to continue with them until their main job provides more income.

In response to high costs, more working young adults are living with their parents.

A growing number are also focusing on how they can thrive when companies reward owners and shareholders more than workers. Labor compensation as a share of non-farm GDP fell to 52.9% in the second quarter this year, "the lowest level in the series which begins in the first quarter of 1947," according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

One result of this shift in awareness has been a sixfold increase in investing by younger people since 2015, catalyzed by technology that has made the stock market more accessible. In 2024, 37% of 25-year-olds had moved money into investment accounts since age 22, up from 6% in 2015, according to the JPMorganChase Institute.

Even so, many young workers are not yet participating in the stock market. Some don't know how to, and others cannot afford to.

Still, "it's never been more obvious that wealth begets wealth," economic commentator Kyla Scanlon, who is herself a member of Gen Z, recently wrote, noting that since 1990, median pay has increased by 18%, home prices by 66%, and S&P 500 SPX returns by 1,500%. "Wealth - ownership - feels like it matters more than any sort of labor income, because wealth builds more wealth."

Nicole Ingham, at 33 a young millennial or "zillennial," said her parents always taught her to save money, but never taught her about investing.

Her parents, who were in the military, "were able to get to financial prosperity through hard work and grit and determination," she said. "I want ease, and I want space, and I want time. And those are things my parents never had." Because she didn't have the job security or pension that comes with a military career, she worried that simply working and saving would tether her to "the middle-class trap: working until 65 and still not able to retire," she said.

After being exposed to investing through a job at a financial-technology company, Ingham said she "became pretty obsessed with the idea of buying my life back." She started investing most of her salary while she and her husband lived off his $65,000 income, the larger of the two.

Their investable net worth now is just over $1 million, which is in sector-based and total-market index funds as well as individual stocks. This has allowed Ingham to step away from her corporate job and start her own business as a financial coach in Jacksonville, Fla. She plans to hire their two children to do work for her company to jump-start their ability to build wealth, with the aim of setting them up to be multimillionaires by the time they retire.

"As soon as you figure it out, it's like the secret is out, and you're like, 'Oh, there's another way,'" Ingham said.

Kaylee Archibald, age 31, said she has been able to invest about 25% to 30% of her gross income by advocating for higher pay at her job and doing odd jobs such as reselling clothing and pet sitting. "I was lucky enough to have a couple of really great co-workers that pushed me to ask for more [pay]" at work, she told MarketWatch. She mostly invests in index funds such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF VOO, Invesco QQQ Trust QQQ and Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF VTI.

"I'm hoping if I stay on track that I'll be work-optional in 10 years," Archibald said. Her father thinks that is "unfathomable," but she believes that by "being intentional now, and investing and saving aggressively, it will change my life."

Outcomes like these, however, are rare. The problem, even for motivated investors, is that for the many people who cannot afford to save aggressively, "steadily investing money into a diversified basket of stocks is a wonderful way to save for your retirement, but it is not a guarantee for getting ahead," said Moore.

Others are exploring entrepreneurship. More than half of Gen Z-ers said they have seriously considered starting a business in the last 12 months, nearly twice the rate of all respondents in a recent poll.

While nearly half of small businesses fail within five years, Kyla Scanlon noted that ownership also affords greater opportunity.

For Will Freeman, age 29, getting ahead meant starting his own consulting firm while working full time. He left his job in 2024, sold his company in 2025 and now works part time as a chief information officer in Tampa.

"I make three times as much as I did at my corporate job and work half the amount of time," he told MarketWatch. While many of his friends went back to school for their MBAs with the goal of working at big consulting firms, he said, "I was already progressing in my career enough, and I didn't have that barrier to getting promoted or creating opportunities for myself."

Many Gen Z-ers say they expect their financial situation to improve over the next year, and about 42% expect to do better than their parents, according to an Urban Institute survey.

Yet many no longer see the old playbook as enough to get ahead. As the paths to prosperity change, Nicole Ingham, the zillennial financial coach, said, "all Americans should have the right to be educated on how to benefit from the growth of the U.S. economy."

MarketWatch will not attribute your answers to you by name without your permission.

data.title: The traditional paths to building wealth are becoming less accessible for young Americans. Here's what happened.
data.description:
By Venessa Wong

Generation Z and young millennials are navigating major shifts in the economy that have made it harder to build wealth the way Americans did in the past

The American financial playbook - education, a stable job and homeownership - doesn't work like it once did, forcing many young people to seek new ways to pursue financial security.

To Eric Clark, it seems that a few decades ago, young Americans could "just go to college, and no matter how much debt you got into, you'd be able to find a job and everything was going to work out."

Clark's Gen X parents earned computer science degrees in the 1990s and secured stable jobs with clear trajectories for career growth straight out of college. They were "able to ride the dot-com boom," Clark told MarketWatch.

They also "worked with people who only went to college for two years and then dropped out, but were still able to get corporate white-collar jobs in the tech industry because they had the qualifications," he said. "A lot has changed."

Clark, 23, graduated with a business degree from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte last year. After months of submitting applications, he accepted a sales job paying $50,000 a year with virtually no chance of earning a commission, based on the company's benchmarks.

"When I went to school, it was not the job I envisioned," he said.

This year, he landed a job with a more promising career outlook, managing client accounts at a fintech company. "I'm extremely fortunate," he said. "I see people my age and older that are having terrible times in the job market."

New American Playbook: New rules for a new generation - and its money

Generation Z, whose members now range in age from 14 to 29, and younger millennials are navigating major shifts in the U.S. economy that have made the traditional paths to building wealth in America - education, a stable job and homeownership - less accessible. Artificial intelligence is threatening the future of entry-level jobs in the fields many people study in college. First-time home buyers face prices for starter homes that their incomes cannot cover. Consumer debt is ballooning.

Meanwhile, an entry-level salary doesn't buy the kind of life it did when Clark's parents were entering the workforce.

Those changes are forcing young adults to adjust their expectations and figure out other ways to build financial security. Many are renting longer, and those who can are investing earlier, focusing on passive income streams and developing multiple sources of income.

Young Americans are "experiencing some macroeconomic shifts that are, in a lot of ways, unprecedented," JP Julien, a partner at McKinsey and leader of the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility, told MarketWatch. "They're entering a labor market that is increasingly challenging for entry-level roles in light of AI ... and facing head-on a massive affordability challenge."

In a new study from the research group, young people cited the rising cost of living as the most common barrier to economic mobility. They also said financial security was their top aspiration.

It's a shift that Mechele Dickerson, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law and the author of a recent book titled "The Middle-Class New Deal," has witnessed as her students - and her own children, who are now in their 20s - try to make their way as independent adults.

"It's becoming increasingly hard for lower- and middle-income young adults to become and remain middle class, and to attain the markers of the middle class," Dickerson told MarketWatch. Such markers include a college degree, a stable job, savings for short- and long-term goals, and homeownership.

Incomes are not keeping pace with many expenses, she said, and "if you can't afford to buy a house" or achieve other common financial goals, "the earnings don't make you feel any better."

How the old formula for prosperity broke down

The traditional path for young people to succeed began to erode long ago.

The benchmarks for the contemporary understanding of the American middle class evolved in the 20th century, said Sam Pizzigati, an associate fellow at the Institute for Policy Studies, a progressive think tank.

Previously, "middle class" generally referred to workers - "doctors, lawyers, shopkeepers, that sat between the rich at the top and the vast majority of Americans at the bottom who had no savings, no homes of their own, and precious little education," he said.

But from 1940 to 1960, a number of forces - a boom in home building following World War II, low-interest loans provided through the G.I. Bill (which mainly went to white veterans), government funding to expand public universities and community colleges, and a strong labor movement - reshaped America's middle class into an educated group that was prosperous enough to buy a home and still have money for discretionary spending each month, often thanks to jobs that promised retirement security through a pension.

"The idea that average working people could afford homes of their own was so exotic," Pizzigati said.

But the middle class entered a prolonged period of weakening in the 1970s. Despite long periods of economic growth in the 1980s and 1990s, income growth, and wealth, was increasingly concentrated among the highest earners.

Wages stagnated, government funding for college was replaced with an expanded federal student-loan program, credit-card use increased, and debt became a larger part of the middle-class playbook.

Much of that debt was for housing, which historically had been "the way that low- and moderate-income American households built wealth," said Richard Fry, a senior researcher at Pew Research Center. Even today, aside from making a mortgage payment - which functions as a sort of forced-savings mechanism - households typically don't save much at all, he noted. Many don't even have retirement accounts.

Household debt grew from 45% of gross domestic product in 1965 to about 100% in 2007, at the height of the housing bubble. Prospective home buyers who would not have qualified for a loan in previous decades were approved - sometimes without having to verify their income or assets - during the subprime-mortgage boom in the 2000s, with disastrous economic consequences.

Gen Z-ers grew up in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, which exposed the flaws of the debt-centric tool kit that had been offered to the middle class. It was the first time since the post-World War II economic boom that there was a large-scale, nationwide loss of middle-class wealth through housing.

A painfully slow economic recovery followed in the 2010s. Many newly graduated millennials were underemployed, working jobs that didn't require a college degree.

"A lot of people went off and got degrees, especially overpriced degrees," Joseph S. Moore, the author of a new book titled "How to Get Rich in American History," told MarketWatch. "We overproduced elite candidates, but there weren't that many elite jobs to begin with - and they're starting to shrink."

New businesses scaled up using gig workers, who were not offered stable hours, pay or benefits. It took nearly nine years - until 2016 - for the median income to recover to pre-recession levels.

The Federal Reserve characterized the period from 2007 to 2016 as a "wealthless recovery" for all but the richest Americans, as rates of homeownership and stock-market participation fell for low- and middle-income households.

On the heels of the COVID-19 pandemic, the oldest members of Gen Z embarked on their adult lives only to face an affordability crisis that touched everything from education to housing and childcare to groceries - and that continues today.

Meanwhile, AI began to emerge as a major challenge to employment, especially for those just starting out in the workforce.

Today, half of Gen Z-ers say their college degree was a waste of money.

As a result of all these shifts, the 20th-century markers of middle-class life may no longer be relevant in the 21st century, said UT Austin's Mechele Dickerson.

"The world that young people are facing" is not as straightforward as it was for many older Americans, she said. "It may be that the American dream of homeownership [becomes] the American dream of affordable housing."

The financial challenges young people face deserve more attention, she said. "Political leaders at every level - local, state and federal - need to come up with one thing they could do to make it easier for a young adult to become and remain middle class."

How young Americans are dealing with a broken playbook

Despite facing notable challenges and coming of age in a culture infected by "big woe," or an onslaught of despairing information, Moore believes there is still reason for young people to be optimistic.

"We have this illusion that what the baby boomer generation did, if it worked for them, it therefore must always have worked, and that's just not true," he said. This "doesn't mean nothing works. It just means different things work" in different eras.

Young adults may face new headwinds, but some of them will also benefit from new tailwinds, Moore added.

As Eric Clark, the recent grad, sees it, "there are some issues young people are facing that you can course-correct for." Some people he knows went into blue-collar professions, for example, and "it's worked out great." Yet there are other issues "that are out of our hands," he said. "There's no amount of personal responsibility that is going to fix the housing market."

Today's young people are questioning the old playbook: Get an expensive degree to land a good job and buy a home, even if that means loading up on debt. In many cases, they want money, and to cope with financial pressures, they want it fast.

data.title: Real Estate Expert "King" Gary Cox Breaks Down Comparative Market Analysis in HelloNation
data.description:
Real Estate Expert "King" Gary Cox Breaks Down Comparative Market Analysis in HelloNation

Real Estate Expert "King" Gary Cox Breaks Down Comparative Market Analysis in HelloNation

PR Newswire

ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Sept. 11, 2026

In HelloNation, Real Estate Expert "King" Gary Cox of Anchorage, Alaska Explains How a Comparative Market Analysis Reveals a Home's True Value.

ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Sept. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What determines a home's true market value? A HelloNation article explains how a comparative market analysis offers a more accurate answer than automated online estimates.

The HelloNation article explains that many homeowners start with an automated online estimate, since it appears the moment they search their address. That figure often looks official but rarely matches what a buyer would actually pay.

Real value, the article notes, comes from a more careful process called a comparative market analysis. An agent studies recent sales of similar homes nearby and adjusts for differences in size, age, and condition.

Location carries more weight than many sellers expect, according to the article. Homes just a few blocks apart can sell for different amounts because of school zones, traffic patterns, or nearby amenities.

Condition matters just as much, the article explains. A home with an updated kitchen or a newer roof tends to outsell a similar property that still needs work.

Specific features shape the final number too. An extra bathroom, a finished basement, a garage, or a fenced yard can each add measurable value based on local buyer demand.

Current competition changes the equation as well, the article points out. When several similar homes are listed nearby, buyers have more choices, while limited inventory tends to draw stronger offers.

The article adds that days on market tell their own story. A home that sells quickly usually reflects strong demand at that price, while one that needs several reductions may be overpriced for the moment.

Real Estate Expert "King" Gary Cox of Alaska Real Estate King is featured in the article. It explains that a local agent typically provides a comparative market analysis at no cost before a home goes on the market.

The agent adjusts each comparable sale up or down based on how it differs from the home being priced, the article explains. A comparable with an extra bedroom might be adjusted downward for comparison, while one without a garage might be adjusted upward.

According to the article, the final report usually includes a suggested price range rather than one fixed number. This differs from automated tools, which rely on public records and broad formulas that can miss a home's true condition.

The article cautions that comparing a home to a neighbor's recent sale can be misleading, since even nearby houses can differ in condition and updates. A Real Estate Expert who understands these local differences can add context that numbers alone cannot provide.

The article, which features Real Estate Expert Cox, notes that pricing accurately from the start tends to produce better results than adjusting later. Homes that begin with a realistic, well supported price often attract stronger interest in the first weeks on the market.

The report's price range approach gives homeowners room to make an informed decision based on timeline and goals, the article explains. A seller who needs to move quickly might price toward the lower end of that range. One with more flexibility might start higher and adjust based on buyer response.

Broader market conditions round out the picture as well, the article notes. Interest rates, buyer demand, and the pace of recent sales all influence how quickly a home moves and at what price.

How a Comparative Market Analysis Determines Home Value features insights from "King" Gary Cox, Real Estate Expert of Anchorage, Alaska, in HelloNation.

Congressional Resolution Honors ACI Centennial and the Essential Role of Cleaning in American Life

  • Rep. Rick Allen Resolution Recognizes American Cleaning Institute’s 100th Anniversary
  • U.S. Cleaning Products Sector Employs Nearly 65,000 Americans and Generates $88 Billion in Economic Output
  • Resolution Spotlights the Industry’s Role in Public Health, Manufacturing, Supply Chain Resilience and Innovation

As the American Cleaning Institute (ACI) celebrates the centennial anniversary of its founding in 1926, U.S. Rep. Rick Allen (R-GA) introduced a congressional resolution honoring 100 years of ACI and recognizing the essential role cleaning and the U.S. cleaning products industry play in protecting health, supporting American jobs and manufacturing, and helping communities thrive.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260911754534/en/

As the American Cleaning Institute (ACI) celebrates the centennial anniversary of its founding in 1926, U.S. Rep. Rick Allen (R-GA) introduced a congressional resolution honoring 100 years of ACI and recognizing the essential role cleaning and the U.S. cleaning products industry play in protecting health, supporting American jobs and manufacturing, and helping communities thrive.

Rep. Allen is a leading member of the House Energy & Commerce Committee and has been a champion for policy issues critical to the cleaning products sector, including by working to ensure that federal regulatory processes reflect the industry’s innovative use of new and existing chemistries in consumer and industrial products.

Rep. Allen’s resolution recognizes the economic contributions of cleaning product manufacturers, suppliers and distributors across all 50 states, including nearly 65,000 Americans employed by the sector and $88 billion in annual economic activity. It also recognizes the everyday value of cleaning, sanitizing and disinfecting products – from protecting health in homes, schools and healthcare facilities to supporting workplaces, manufacturing operations and the many shared spaces on which communities depend.

“The cleaning products industry provides more than 3,000 jobs and $3.3 billion in economic output in the state of Georgia. Whether it is a home, business, school, hospital, or other setting, all Americans rely on cleaning products daily. I am proud to recognize the 100th anniversary of the American Cleaning Institute and look forward to its continued success in the years and decades to come,” said Rep. Allen.

“This resolution recognizes not only ACI’s 100-year history, but the enduring value of cleaning in American life and the people and companies who make that possible,” said Jennifer Abril, ACI President and CEO. “As we enter our second century, ACI is focused on a future where cleaning is recognized as essential to healthy living and thriving communities.

“That means advancing the science of cleaning, supporting sound public policy, enabling continued innovation and helping ensure that people and institutions have access to the products they rely on every day.

“We appreciate Rep. Allen’s recognition of this milestone and of an industry whose work touches every American, every day.”

Founded in 1926 as the Association of American Soap and Glycerine Producers, ACI has evolved alongside the products, science and technologies that have transformed how Americans clean. The organization became the Soap and Detergent Association in 1960 and the American Cleaning Institute in 2010, reflecting an expanding industry and the increasingly important role cleaning plays across homes, businesses, schools, healthcare facilities and other institutional settings. As ACI enters its second century, that evolution continues with a renewed focus on advancing the science and value of cleaning.

The American Cleaning Institute® (ACI) is the home of the U.S. cleaning products industry and represents the $88 billion U.S. cleaning products market. ACI members include the formulators of soaps, detergents and general cleaning products used in household, commercial, industrial and institutional settings; companies that supply ingredients and finished packaging for these products; and chemical distributors. ACI serves the growth and innovation of the U.S. cleaning products industry by advancing the health and quality of life of people and protecting the planet.

data.title: KBRA Assigns Preliminary Ratings to OnDeck Asset Securitization IV, LLC, Series 2026-1
data.description:
KBRA Assigns Preliminary Ratings to OnDeck Asset Securitization IV, LLC, Series 2026-1

KBRA assigns preliminary ratings to notes issued by OnDeck Asset Securitization IV, LLC (“ODAS IV” or the “Issuer”). ODAS IV will issue four classes of Series 2026-1 Notes (“ODAS IV 2026-1”) totaling $500.02 million.

On Deck Capital Inc., which was founded in 2006, and ODK Capital, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of Enova International, Inc. formed in December 2020, (collectively “OnDeck” or the “Company”) operates through an online lending platform (www.ondeck.com) (the “OnDeck Platform”) to originate small business loans in the U.S. through its subsidiaries. The Company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Enova International, Inc. (“Enova”), a non-prime consumer and small business lender. Enova is a publicly traded fintech company under the ticker “ENVA”. Since its founding, OnDeck has originated over $29 billion to over 206,000 small businesses. OnDeck had 388 dedicated personnel as of July 2026.

ODAS IV 2026-1 represents OnDeck’s eleventh small business ABS securitization. The transaction issued $500.02 million of Series 2026-1 notes (the “Series 2026-1 Notes” or the “Notes”) secured by a revolving pool of Receivables that were underwritten under OnDeck’s credit guidelines and originated through the OnDeck Platform to small businesses in the U.S. ODAS IV 2026-1 features a revolving period (the “Revolving Period”), which will end on the earlier of (i) the close of business on September 30, 2028 or (ii) the date on which an Amortization Event has occurred. The proceeds of the sale of the Series 2026-1 Notes will be used to fund the Series 2026-1 reserve account and to purchase fixed-rate small business loans that are either the Term Loans or funded portions of the LOCs originated through the OnDeck Platform.

KBRA applied its Global General Rating Methodology for Asset-Backed Securities as well as its Global Structured Finance Counterparty Methodology as part of its analysis of the transaction’s underlying collateral pool and the proposed capital structure. This transaction falls within “Category 1 – Financial Assets” categorization noted within the General Global Rating Methodology for Asset Backed Securities, which typically relates to transactions that are backed by pools of consumer or commercial financial obligations owed by diverse obligors. KBRA considered its operational review of the Company, as well as periodic update calls with the Company. Operative agreements and legal opinions will be reviewed prior to closing.

data.title: Nymex Overview: Petroleum Futures Falling, But Still on Track for Large Weekly Gains — OPIS
data.description:
Crude oil and refined product futures prices were falling Friday morning, but they remained on track to end the week with substantial gains amid ongoing uncertainty over global energy supply due to renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.

The week's increase in futures prices is being felt by U.S. motorists, with retail diesel prices across the country topping $6/gal for the first time ever.

U.S. oil prices moved back below $100/bbl Friday morning, with the October NYMEX West Texas Intermediate crude contract falling by $2.95 to $99.53/bbl, still about $8 higher than last Friday's settlement. November WTI prices were $2.99 lower to $95.41/bbl.

Brent crude futures were seeing similar losses for the day, with the November futures contract falling by $3.05 to $104.58/bbl, also up about $8 for the week. December Brent was trading $3.05 higher to $99.67/bbl.

RBOB futures were leading refined products lower, with October futures seeing losses of 5.63cts to $3.3369/gal. That's about 13cts above last Friday's finish. November prices were down by 5.98cts to $3.1465/gal.

ULSD futures were seeing lighter losses, with the October contract trading down 3.69cts to $5.0206/gal and November prices off by 3.93cts to $4.8066/gal. Prices are up about 46cts/gal for the week.

U.S. retail diesel prices started Friday averaging $6.0556/gal, an increase of 7.83cts overnight and the first time prices have risen above $6/gal. Retail prices are more than 20cts/gal higher than last Friday.

Friday's decline in petroleum prices comes even as tensions remain high in the Middle East, with Iran this week targeting U.S. Navy ships and the U.S. retaliating by striking Iranian tankers. Meanwhile, Iranian-backed Houthi fighters on Friday captured Mayun Island at the entrance to the Red Sea, according to reports. That could potentially cause further disruptions to oil shipments from the region.

Weighing on energy prices is data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showing consumer prices rose by 3.4% in August, raising the possibility the U.S. Federal Reserve will approve hiking interest rates to slow inflation.
